title: Short Stuff: Emperor Norton
summary: Short Stuff episode on Emperor Norton (Joshua Norton), the eccentric self-proclaimed "Emperor of the United States" who lived in San Francisco. Covers his English birth and South African upbringing, his rise as a wealthy San Francisco businessman, his 1852 rice corner that failed after more ships arrived from Peru and led to bankruptcy, his reemergence as Emperor Norton with proclamations printed by the San Francisco Bulletin, his military-style uniform, dogs Bummer and Lazarus, his added title Protector of Mexico, his decrees (abolishing Congress, dissolving the parties, the "Frisco" fine, the Oakland-San Francisco bridge and tunnel survey), his own currency and free meals, his death in 1880 and large funeral and reburial, and his later presence in Mark Twain's work, operas, a musical, and a Bonanza episode.

segments.title: Introduction and early life
segments.summary: The hosts introduce Emperor Norton as an early San Francisco eccentric, covering his English birth, South African childhood, arrival in San Francisco, and quick rise to wealth in real estate.

segments.title: The rice corner and bankruptcy
segments.summary: After a Chinese rice export ban in 1852, Norton bought a shipment of rice from Peru expecting to corner the market, but more ships arrived, prices fell, and he went bankrupt.

segments.title: Emperor Norton's proclamations and the Bulletin
segments.summary: After reemerging with a changed demeanor, Norton declared himself Emperor of the United States. The San Francisco Bulletin printed his proclamation, starting a local media tradition of reporting on him.

segments.title: Uniform, dogs, and Protector of Mexico
segments.summary: Norton wore a military uniform with epaulets from Presidio officers and a peacock-feather hat, and was accompanied by dogs Bummer and Lazarus. In 1861 he added the title Protector of Mexico after the French invasion.

segments.title: Decrees, Frisco ban, and the Oakland bridge survey
segments.summary: The hosts describe Norton's decrees, including calls to abolish Congress and the parties, a fine for calling San Francisco Frisco, and an 1872 survey for connecting Oakland and San Francisco, which later came true with the Bay Bridge and a transit tunnel.

segments.title: Currency, free meals, and death
segments.summary: Norton issued his own currency, which was accepted, and ate free at the city's best restaurants. He died at age 61 on a street corner in 1880, with few possessions found in his room.

segments.title: Funeral, reburial, and legacy
segments.summary: The Pacific Club arranged a rosewood casket and a funeral procession that thousands attended. His later reburial in Colma drew a large crowd, and he has been featured in Mark Twain's writing, operas, a musical, and a Bonanza episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and give the standard show sign-off.
